tier_reason: The README table ('More Performant Than Float128, BigFloat') gives first-party relative times for Double64 versus Float128 (libquadmath) and BigFloat at 128 bits (MPFR), produced with BenchmarkTools 'on one machine', with no hardware, Julia version, absolute times or linked benchmark script, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Relative time, smaller is faster, Double64 = 1. Versus Big128 (BigFloat/MPFR at 128 bits): dot(v,v) 7, v .+ v 16, v .* v 25, exp.(m) 6, m * m 9, det(m) 11. Versus Float128 (libquadmath via Quadmath.jl): dot(v,v) 3, v .+ v 7, v .* v 12, exp.(m) 2, m * m 3, det(m) 5. Vectors of 1000 values, 50x50 matrices.
corrections.caveats: Table in the README has no hardware, Julia version, absolute times or benchmark script, only relative ratios from BenchmarkTools 'on one machine'. Not an equal-precision comparison: Double64 carries about 106 significand bits (the README says 85+ accurate bits) with Float64 exponent range and no correct rounding, while Big128 is correctly rounded 128-bit MPFR and Float128 has 6 more significant bits and a far wider exponent range. Compares against MPFR only through Julia's allocating BigFloat wrapper. Pure Julia package, not callable from C++ without embedding Julia; the like-for-like C++ library is QD (double-double/quad-double). MultiFloats.jl (separate entry) claims to be 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl.

notes: All six Big128 ratios match the README exactly; I added the Float128 column from the same table. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 172 stars, not archived, default branch main, last commit 2026-07-28 (active). Julia-only package; the orchestrator may want to tag it as off-language for a C++ list.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark against scalar MPFR 4.2.1 with public code (tests/cgbnbench.c, 'gmake bench-cgbn'), the GPU model, CUDA 13.2, nvcc flags and host GCC 14.3.1 (design PDF), but the CPU model of the baseline core and the host CFLAGS are never stated, so it cannot be A; not peer reviewed, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 13.2 (driver 595.71.05) with NVCCFLAGS '-O3 -arch=$cuda_arch -Xcompiler -fPIC' (configure default arch 'native', sm_120 on the test GPU); host compiler GCC 14.3.1 per the design PDF's test-system table, but CFLAGS for the MPFR baseline are not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party measurements on a single machine; the CPU model is never given (README or design PDF), and the baseline is one core of scalar MPFR, so a multi-core MPFR run would shrink the ratios by up to the core count. A single operation (n = 1) is always a loss, about 3x to 1570x slower than the CPU (derived from page data); addition never wins in batch mode (every add batch cell is 0.7x or lower); the README's Limitations section says division and square root above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU. The repository is one 'Initial Github commit' (2026-09-12) of an MPFR 4.2.1 tree plus the GPU backend; no sign of upstream MPFR adoption was found, although the new source files carry the stock FSF/INRIA MPFR copyright header. The top-level LICENSE file is the GPL-3.0 text (as in upstream MPFR), while the library sources, including the new src/mpfr-cgbn.c and tests/cgbnbench.c, are LGPL-3.0-or-later. Uses CGBN beyond its documented maximum size (above 32768 bits), checked by tests/cgbn-verify.

notes: Every peak figure in claimed_speedup matches the README's own summary and its tables (batch: div 30.4x, sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152, fma 18.3x at 40960, n = 1024; resident at n = 16384: fma 284.1x, mul 230.3x, div 157.1x, add 120.1x, sqrt 114.8x). Results are claimed to be bit-identical to MPFR (rounding, ternary value, flags), checked by tests/tcgbn. Lead for the orchestrator: arXiv 2608.00085 (an MPFR/MPC port to CUDA, about 40-105x per a search snippet) was seen in search results but not opened.

tier_reason: The README's 30x/6x/2x claims against BigFloat (MPFR), Quadmath.jl and DoubleFloats.jl are first-party with no table, hardware, Julia version or linked script. The peer-reviewed SC25 paper could not be opened (theory.stanford.edu, dl.acm.org and arxiv.org are blocked here), and its public harness (dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks) benchmarks a separate C++ header rather than this Julia package, so it stays C.

corrections.caveats: README gives bare ratios ('at 30-digit precision ... 30x faster than BigFloat, 6x faster than Quadmath.jl, 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl') without a table, hardware, Julia version or version of the package measured. The current v3.0 README no longer links the benchmark gist (gist.github.com/dzhang314/3e10463843f4ab5f5a4a2206c877771b, MultiFloatsBenchmark.jl: QR of 400x400 and pseudoinverse of 250x400 at about 106 bits); the gist has code but no recorded output. Correctness history: the README says the v2.0 algorithms for Float64x5-Float64x8 were 'fundamentally broken' (types removed in v3.0), v2.0 had denormalization issues causing spurious accuracy losses, and prevfloat/nextfloat skipped values before v3.0. Treats +-Inf inputs as NaN; transcendental functions go through MPFR. Compared against MPFR only through Julia's allocating BigFloat. Pure Julia package, not callable from C++ without embedding Julia. The SC25 paper (Zhang and Aiken, doi 10.1145/3712285.3759876) reportedly measures a C++ prototype of the same algorithms against QD, CAMPARY, MPFR and FLINT, but it was not opened.

notes: Claim text matches the README verbatim; metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 159 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-16 (active). Strong lead for a separate C++ entry: github.com/dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks (MIT) contains a header-only C++ MultiFloats.hpp (multifloats/) plus Google Benchmark harnesses for MPFR, GMP, FLINT, CLN, QD, CAMPARY, Boost and libquadmath, built with g++-14 / clang++-20 '-O3 -march=native -flto -ffp-contract=off -fopenmp' (build_linux.sh). Search snippets credit the SC25 paper with up to 35.6x over MPFR, 11.7x over QD, 34.4x over CAMPARY and 41.4x over FLINT on AMD Zen 5. That could reach B, or A if the paper names the CPU model, but I did not open the paper.
